title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Introduction
content: The study of drug elimination kinetics has been a cornerstone of pharmacology since the early to mid-20th century, when researchers first recognized that certain drugs do not follow proportional elimination patterns at high concentrations. [1] Early experiments with alcohol, salicylates, and barbiturates demonstrated that high doses can saturate the body's elimination systems, producing nonlinear removal. For example, alcohol is metabolized primarily by hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase, which becomes saturated even at moderate blood alcohol levels, resulting in a constant elimination rate independent of plasma concentration. Similarly, salicylates follow first-order elimination at low doses but transition to zero-order kinetics at higher doses, leading to accumulation and potential toxicity. These findings laid the groundwork for modern pharmacokinetics, which classifies drugs based on how their elimination rates are influenced by plasma concentration. These core principles remain essential for safely prescribing medications such as antibiotics, chemotherapeutics, anticoagulants, sedatives, and anticonvulsants. [2]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Introduction
content: Among the pioneers of quantitative pharmacokinetics, Erik M P Widmark provided one of the first mathematical descriptions of ethanol absorption, distribution, and elimination, demonstrating that ethanol elimination becomes capacity-limited at higher concentrations. Observations that aspirin, phenobarbital, and other barbiturates also exhibit saturable metabolism further prompted the development of predictive models for plasma concentrations and dosing. Over time, these studies evolved into frameworks describing first-, zero-, and mixed-order kinetics, enabling clinicians to anticipate drug behavior and accurately individualize therapy. [3]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Introduction
content: Elimination kinetics describe how the body removes drugs over time. In first-order kinetics, the rate of elimination is proportional to plasma concentration, meaning a constant fraction of the drug is metabolized or excreted per unit time. This phenomenon produces an exponential decline in drug levels, with the half-life remaining constant regardless of dose. [4] In zero-order kinetics, elimination occurs at a constant rate independent of plasma concentration, typically when metabolic or excretory pathways are saturated. In such cases, the time required to reduce plasma concentration by half depends on the starting concentration, making dosing predictions more complex. Recognizing these differences is essential in clinical decision-making, as the type of elimination kinetics influences therapeutic effectiveness, the risk of toxic accumulation, and dosing adjustments in special populations. [5]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Introduction
content: For simplicity, this discussion applies a one-compartment model, treating the human body as a single homogeneous system for drug distribution and elimination. [6] Although most drugs follow first-order kinetics at therapeutic concentrations, some shift to zero-order kinetics at higher concentrations or under certain physiological conditions. Understanding these transitions is critical for predicting drug behavior, avoiding toxicity, and optimizing therapy.

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Issues of Concern
content: Understanding how a substance is eliminated is critical for safe medication administration and the management of toxic exposures. In poisoning or overdose scenarios, identifying elimination kinetics enables early intervention, predicts toxic accumulation, and dictates therapeutic options, including activated charcoal, hemodialysis, or antidote administration. For instance, in methanol ingestion, toxicity results primarily from metabolites such as formic acid. Because methanol elimination is zero-order (at higher doses), the elapsed time since ingestion, rather than the total dose ingested, determines the urgency of interventions such as ethanol or fomepizole therapy, which competitively inhibit metabolism and prevent the formation of toxic metabolites. [6] [7]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Issues of Concern
content: Drugs following zero-order kinetics are eliminated at a constant amount per unit time, whereas those following first-order kinetics are cleared proportionally to plasma concentration. Failure to recognize these patterns can lead to inappropriate dosing or unexpected toxicity. Phenytoin exemplifies this risk, as its saturable hepatic metabolism means that small increases in dose can result in disproportionately high plasma concentrations, potentially causing neurologic toxicity even when doses appear therapeutic. Similarly, large doses of salicylates in adults can overwhelm metabolic pathways, producing severe acid-base disturbances, hyperventilation, and neurological effects. Other substances, including ethanol, theophylline, and certain chemotherapeutic agents, also display nonlinear kinetics under specific circumstances, highlighting the importance of clinician awareness. [8]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Issues of Concern
content: Even when the ingested substance is unknown, serial plasma or blood measurements can help characterize elimination patterns. Clinicians must also consider patient-specific factors, including age, liver and kidney function, comorbid conditions, and concomitant medications, all of which can alter drug kinetics and increase the risk of adverse effects.

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Cellular Level
content: Drug elimination at the cellular level reflects the interplay between physiological capacity and enzymatic machinery. Hepatocytes, the primary liver cells, metabolize drugs through phase I and II reactions. Phase I enzymes, mainly cytochrome P450 (CYP) isoforms, introduce polar functional groups via oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis. These reactions often follow first-order kinetics under normal concentrations, as the rate of metabolism is proportional to substrate availability. Phase II enzymes, such as UDP-glucuronyltransferases, sulfotransferases, and glutathione S-transferases, conjugate metabolites, increasing water solubility for renal excretion. When substrate concentrations exceed enzymatic capacity, the system becomes saturated, producing zero-order kinetics, in which a constant amount of drug is metabolized per unit time regardless of plasma concentration. [9]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Cellular Level
content: In the renal tubular epithelium, drugs and metabolites are cleared through glomerular filtration, passive diffusion, and active secretion via organic anion and cation transporters. Most drugs at therapeutic levels follow first-order kinetics because transporter capacity is not exceeded: higher plasma concentrations lead to proportionally faster elimination. However, drugs dependent on saturable transporters, such as specific antivirals, aminoglycosides, and high-dose methotrexate, can transition to zero-order kinetics when transporter capacity is maximized. [10]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Cellular Level
content: Cellular cofactors such as NADPH, UDP-glucuronic acid, and glutathione are essential for enzymatic reactions. Depletion of these cofactors can further limit metabolic capacity, effectively reducing the elimination rate. Drug-drug interactions at the cellular level, such as competitive inhibition of enzymes or transporters, can reduce clearance and shift first-order processes toward zero-order kinetics. [11]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Cellular Level
content: Genetic variability and disease states further influence cellular elimination. [12] Polymorphisms in CYP isoenzymes or renal transporters produce interindividual differences in drug clearance and susceptibility to toxicity. Pathological conditions such as hepatic fibrosis, cholestasis, or acute tubular necrosis impair cellular machinery, reducing elimination efficiency and altering expected kinetic patterns. [13] [14]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Cellular Level
content: By connecting cellular function to systemic pharmacokinetics, zero- and first-order kinetics are revealed as direct outcomes of physiological capacity and enzymatic or transporter activity. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for predicting drug behavior, optimizing dosing, and anticipating transitions between kinetic patterns. Drugs exhibiting zero-order kinetics, such as phenytoin and theophylline, require therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) because plasma concentrations are not predictable from dose alone, making TDM essential for safe dosing adjustments. [15] [16] Routine antimicrobial TDM in critically ill patients is required, even when drugs have different kinetics, because critical illness alters drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination, leading to unpredictable plasma concentrations and increasing the risk of treatment failure or toxicity. [17] [16] [18]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Organ Systems Involved
content: Drug elimination relies primarily on the liver and kidneys. The liver metabolizes drugs through phase I (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) and phase II (conjugation with glucuronide, sulfate, or glutathione) reactions, converting lipophilic substances into water-soluble metabolites suitable for renal excretion. Saturation of these pathways can shift elimination from first- to zero-order kinetics, particularly for drugs such as phenytoin or high-dose aspirin. Hepatic enzyme activity is influenced by genetic polymorphisms, medication-prompted induction or inhibition, and disease states, all of which can dramatically affect elimination rates. [19]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Organ Systems Involved
content: In the kidneys, drugs and metabolites are processed through glomerular filtration, tubular secretion, and tubular reabsorption, which together determine the extent of urinary excretion. Impaired renal function prolongs drug half-life, especially for substances that are excreted unchanged, such as aminoglycosides or lithium. Other organs contribute modestly to elimination; for example, the lungs exhale volatile anesthetics, and minor amounts of other substances are excreted in sweat or saliva. [20] Some drugs are cleared via biliary excretion into the small intestine and are subsequently eliminated in feces. Rifampin and ceftriaxone are notable examples that can have important clinical consequences; at high doses, ceftriaxone may precipitate in the gallbladder and form biliary sludge, which can cause cholecystitis or biliary colic, particularly in neonates or with prolonged therapy. [21] [22]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Organ Systems Involved
content: Overall, drug elimination is governed by the combined processes of metabolism and excretion. Enzyme activity, renal function, transporter saturation, and drug interactions determine whether a drug follows first- or zero-order kinetics. [23] Clinicians must consider these organ-level contributions when predicting drug behavior, designing dosing schedules, and preventing toxicity.

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Function
content: The principal difference between zero- and first-order kinetics lies in how elimination rates are impacted by plasma concentration. In zero-order kinetics, a fixed amount of drug is eliminated per unit time, producing a linear decline in plasma concentration. A helpful analogy is a fixed-size pipe draining water from a tank: no matter how much water is present, the pipe can remove only a set volume per minute. Time, not concentration, limits the rate of elimination.

This mechanism is comparable to a pipe with unlimited capacity: the more water there is in the tank, the faster it flows out; here, plasma concentration is the limiting factor.

content: First-order elimination can transition to zero-order when metabolic or excretory systems become saturated. Drugs such as theophylline, phenytoin, and ethanol exemplify this principle. Monitoring plasma levels and adjusting dosing are essential in such cases to prevent toxicity. [24] [10]

content: Both zero- and first-order kinetics are derived from the same general equation (see Image. Zero- and First-Order Elimination and Equations). In the kinetic order elimination equation, Δ[drug] represents the change in plasma drug concentration over time, n represents the order of elimination (1 for first-order, 0 for zero-order), and −Kc is a constant.

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Mechanism
content: When n = 1 (first-order), the rate of change in plasma concentration is proportional to the amount of drug present, meaning the initial concentration is the rate-limiting factor. When n = 0 (zero-order), the change in plasma concentration is constant, equal to −Kc, so the rate-limiting factor is time.

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Mechanism
content: Mathematical modeling of these kinetics allows clinicians to calculate half-life, clearance, and dosing regimens tailored to individual patients. For drugs that transition from first- to zero-order kinetics, Michaelis-Menten kinetics can be applied to predict saturation points and optimize safe dosing. [25] [26] [27] To better understand elimination kinetics, it is essential to review the fundamentals of pharmacokinetics. The equations are given below.

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Mechanism -- Plasma concentration:
content: C = C0 − (k0 × t) C = concentration at time t; C0 = initial concentration; k0 = zero-order rate constant; t = time.

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Mechanism -- Elimination rate (dC/dt):
content: dC/dt = −k0 The rate of change remains constant, regardless of plasma concentration.

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Mechanism -- Zero-order rate constant:
content: k0 = −(dC/dt) Units: mg/L/h, mg/kg/h, or other units of amount per time (NOT reciprocal time).

content: t½ = C0 / (2 × k0) Half-life is variable and depends on initial concentration (NOT a constant).

content: CL = k0 / C Apparent clearance decreases as concentration increases (inverse relationship).

content: t (total) = C0 / k0 Time needed to eliminate all drugs from the body.

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Mechanism -- Michaelis-Menten equation (enzyme saturation model):
content: V = (Vmax × C) / (Km + C) V = enzyme reaction velocity (rate of drug elimination) Vmax = maximum velocity (maximum elimination capacity when the enzyme is 100% saturated) C = substrate concentration (plasma drug concentration) Km = Michaelis constant (Km = concentration at which V = ½ Vmax)

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Mechanism
content: Most drug-metabolizing enzymes follow classic Michaelis-Menten kinetics, producing a hyperbolic curve where reaction velocity rises with substrate concentration until saturation. In some cases, enzymes exhibit sigmoidal kinetics due to allosteric inhibition, in which substrate binding at one site affects activity at other sites.

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Pathophysiology
content: Pathophysiological conditions can shift drug kinetics from first-order toward zero-order or mixed-order. Hepatic diseases such as cirrhosis, fibrosis, or cholestasis reduce CYP-mediated metabolism, leading to the accumulation of hepatically metabolized drugs such as phenytoin, theophylline, and acetaminophen. In these disease states, saturable enzymes can reach capacity at lower concentrations, producing zero-order kinetics. [28] [29]

Hepatic diseases such as cirrhosis, fibrosis, or cholestasis reduce CYP-mediated metabolism, leading to the accumulation of hepatically metabolized drugs such as phenytoin, theophylline, and acetaminophen. In these disease states, saturable enzymes can reach capacity at lower concentrations, producing zero-order kinetics. [28] [29]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Pathophysiology
content: Renal pathology also alters drug clearance. Acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, or chronic kidney disease can reduce filtration, secretion, or reabsorption efficiency, prolonging the half-life of renally eliminated drugs such as aminoglycosides, digoxin, and lithium. Saturation of remaining transporters may induce nonlinear elimination, thereby compounding the risk of toxicity. [30]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Pathophysiology
content: Genetic polymorphisms in CYP enzymes or renal transporters produce interindividual variability in clearance. For instance, CYP2C9 or CYP2C19 variants reduce the metabolism of certain drugs, predisposing patients to toxicity. When combined with organ impairment, these variations can shift elimination from predictable first-order kinetics to nonlinear or zero-order kinetics.

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Pathophysiology
content: Systemic factors, such as hypoperfusion, inflammation, and sepsis, can further impair hepatic metabolism and renal elimination, causing commonly first-order drugs to behave unpredictably. For this reason, frequent plasma monitoring and individualized dosing are essential in critically ill patients. [31]

For this reason, frequent plasma monitoring and individualized dosing are essential in critically ill patients. [31]

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Clinical Significance
content: Understanding elimination kinetics is vital for patient care, dosing strategies, and toxicity prevention. Most drugs follow first-order kinetics. For example, beta-lactam antibiotics exhibit predictable exponential decay, allowing clinicians to anticipate plasma concentrations and adjust doses safely. However, drugs with zero-order kinetics, such as ethanol, salicylates, phenytoin, methanol, and theophylline, can accumulate rapidly even at moderate doses. Zero-order elimination also dictates therapeutic options; in methanol poisoning, early intervention depends on the elapsed time rather than the total dose.

title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Clinical Significance
content: High-dose chemotherapy protocols, such as ICE (ifosfamide, carboplatin, and etoposide), illustrate practical applications of elimination kinetics: early plasma monitoring identifies patients at risk of renal toxicity before conventional markers, such as serum creatinine, rise. Similarly, theophylline therapy requires careful monitoring to prevent underdosing or toxicity. title: Physiology, Zero- and First-Order Kinetics -- Clinical Significance
content: Recognizing transitions between kinetic patterns enables individualized therapy, minimizes adverse effects, and optimizes outcomes. [39] [40] Integrating knowledge of elimination kinetics into clinical practice improves medication safety, predicts toxic accumulation, adjusts for organ impairment, and supports effective management of high-risk drugs. These principles exemplify the intersection of physiology and pharmacology in modern medicine.
